title: Bholi
author: K. A. Abbas
summary: Sulekha, the fourth daughter of Numberdar Ramlal, is called Bholi, 'the simpleton'. A fall from her cot at ten months damaged her brain; smallpox at two left her body covered with pock-marks. She could not speak till five and then stammered, so children mocked her and she spoke little. Her parents worried that no one would marry her.

When a primary school for girls opens, the Tehsildar tells Ramlal, as a revenue official, to set an example by sending his daughters. Ramlal's wife says that educated girls cannot be married off, but agrees to send Bholi: there is little chance of her marrying anyway. Bholi is bathed and given a cast-off dress; frightened, she thinks she is being sent away like the cow that was sold.

At school the teacher speaks to her softly, pats her and gives her a picture book. She promises that in a month Bholi will read it, and that if she studies she will lose her stammer and be respected by all. Bholi feels hope for the first time.

Years pass; the village grows into a small town. A rich but lame, middle-aged grocer, Bishamber, with grown-up children, agrees to marry Bholi without dowry. At the wedding he lifts her veil, sees the pock-marks and demands five thousand rupees. To save the family's honour Ramlal pays, putting his turban at Bishamber's feet.

Bholi throws the garland away and refuses to marry so mean and greedy a man. She speaks clearly, without stammering. She tells her father to take back his money and says she will look after her parents in their old age and teach in the school where she studied. The teacher watches with deep satisfaction.
Themes: girls' education, the effect of love and encouragement on a neglected child, dowry and greed, self-respect and empowerment.
K. A. (Khwaja Ahmad) Abbas wrote in English, Hindi and Urdu, wrote the screenplay of Mera Naam Joker and won the National Film Award four times. His autobiography is I Am Not an Island (1977).

Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links the past with the present; simple past for finished actions; past perfect (had + past participle) for the earlier of two past actions. Noun ↔ verb forms (consultation — consult, humiliation — humiliate).

sa2: Why did Bholi talk very little? Give two reasons.
She stammered when she spoke, and other children mimicked and laughed at her. So she lost confidence and kept quiet.
January-February 2021
What were Bholi's mother's views on educating girls?
She believed that girls who went to school could not be married off. She agreed to send Bholi only because she thought Bholi had little chance of marrying anyway.
April 2017
Why was Bholi frightened when she was taken to school?
She had no idea what a school was. Being bathed and given a clean dress reminded her of the cow, Lakshmi, which was washed before being sold, so she feared she was being sent away.
How did the teacher win Bholi's heart on the first day?
She spoke to her in a soft, soothing voice, patted her affectionately, let her say her name slowly and gave her a picture book, promising she would soon read it and be respected.
Why did Ramlal accept Bishamber's proposal though he had doubts?
Bishamber was well-to-do and did not ask for dowry, and no one else was likely to marry Bholi. Ramlal worried about his age, limp and grown-up children, but accepted to settle her future.
Who was responsible for transforming Bholi from a stammering 'dumb cow' into a bold and confident girl?
Her teacher. Her kindness, encouragement and education gave Bholi hope, a voice and self-respect, so that she could refuse a greedy groom.
October 2022
Why did Bholi refuse to marry Bishamber?
He insulted her family by demanding five thousand rupees after seeing her face, and humiliated her father. Bholi would not marry such a mean, greedy and cowardly man.
October 2025
'New clothes had never been made for Bholi.' What does this show about her parents?
It shows that her parents neglected her and treated her as less valuable than her sisters because of her looks and slowness; she got only their cast-off dresses.
October 2017
sa3: 'Going to school was a turning point in Bholi's life.' Elaborate with examples from the story.

Before school Bholi was neglected, mocked and silent. Her teacher's kindness and the promise of reading gave her hope and confidence. Education helped her overcome her stammer, and in the end she spoke boldly, rejected a greedy groom and chose to teach and care for her parents.
Society is by and large insensitive to people who do not fit its idea of 'normal'. Illustrate with reference to Bholi.

Bholi was mocked by children, neglected by her parents and given only old clothes because of her pock-marks and stammer. Her mother called her a dumb cow, and her only proposal came from a lame, greedy old man who still demanded money. Only the teacher saw her worth.

or: What message does the story 'Bholi' convey?

It shows that love, encouragement and education can transform a neglected child. It condemns dowry and the discrimination against girls and the disabled, and celebrates self-respect: an educated Bholi can stand up for herself and her family.

sa3: Describe what happened at Bholi's wedding.

The procession came with a band. When Bishamber lifted the veil and saw the pock-marks, he demanded five thousand rupees. Ramlal paid, laying his turban at his feet. Bholi then threw away the garland, refused to marry so greedy a man, and told her father to take back the money.
